title: Throw Out the Annual Plan
hook: A service menu with seven highlighted offers is not a plan if none of them owns the next 12 weeks.
counterintuition: A bigger annual plan can feel more serious while making execution softer; the useful turn is to shrink the plan until each selected goal forces a near action.
tryThisNow: Circle one goal in your current plan and cross out every listed action that would not matter inside the next 12 weeks.
keyTakeaway: A plan supports execution only when it selects the few 12 week goals and actions that can change what happens this week.

breakdown.fastRead: A service menu with seven marked offers sits beside the old annual plan. The plan looks full, but it cannot tell the team which task comes next. Throwing out the annual plan means cutting away work that only sounds important. 12 Week Planning forces fewer goals, clearer action, and faster proof. Setting Goals matters because the chosen goal has to guide the next move, not just decorate a page.
breakdown.deepRead:
A color-grade timeline frozen at midnight gives Grace a clear problem.

Execution loses force when the annual plan remains the master document. The execution system argues that once the year has been shortened and vision has been made emotionally meaningful, the planning system must also change. The annual plan is too broad for a 12 week execution model. It invites too many priorities, spreads consequence across too much time, and creates the illusion that everything important can stay active together. Throw Out the Annual Plan is therefore not anti-planning. It is anti-mismatch. The target is a plan structure that no longer fits the execution frame. A 12 week system needs a plan built for short-cycle consequence, not a yearly document that keeps overload alive. That is the role of 12 Week Planning. The method treats it as a shift in selectivity, not just in calendar length. A 12 week plan cannot honestly carry the same number of goals the annual plan tried to

The useful test is simple: if the plan cannot tell you what to do this week, it is too loose to govern execution.

Grace can see the cut in practical terms. The color-grade project does not need a full-year wish list; it needs the few scenes that must be finished before the next review. That smaller plan feels less impressive, but it gives the work teeth.
breakdown.fullRead:
Orange cones beside an unrepaired curb shows why a loose annual plan feels safer than a 12 week plan.

Execution architecture changes here. The execution system argues that once the year is shortened and vision has been made emotionally compelling, the annual plan must lose authority. The annual plan is the wrong execution document for a 12 week system because it keeps too many priorities open, tolerates broad ambition without near-term consequence, and weakens the discipline of selection. Throw Out the Annual Plan does not mean abandon planning. It means reject a planning structure that no longer fits the execution model. The annual document belongs to a wide horizon where many goals can remain nominally active at the same time. A 12 week system cannot operate cleanly if that structure stays in control. That is why 12 week planning matters. It changes the unit of execution design. A real 12 week plan is not simply a yearly plan cut down to size. It is a plan built for a tighter window, which means it has to be more selective about commitments, more explicit about the goals that truly matter, and more practical about how progress will be judged before the cycle ends. Setting Goals becomes central under that standard. The standard is strong because it refuses the fantasy that every priority can stay alive together. A good 12 week plan chooses fewer outcomes so execution energy does not get dispersed across too many fronts. Exclusion is not loss here. It is the mechanism that gives a short-cycle plan force. Plan structure is the second half of the argument. The plan has to support execution while there is still time to correct course. It must sit close enough to real work that progress, slippage, and adjustment become visible in time. The official system sequence captures that design: vision sets direction, 12 week goals create focused commitments, and weekly execution keeps the structure operational. The limit also preserves a valuable risk. A reader can easily compress the annual plan into a shorter document and mistake that compression for better

Here is the practical limit. Throwing out the annual plan does not mean throwing out long-term direction. It means refusing to let a distant document pretend to be execution. The long view can still guide the destination, but the 12 week plan has to name the few goals and actions that will receive real attention now.

A plan earns trust when it changes what happens next.

The tradeoff is uncomfortable because a smaller plan exposes what will not be touched. That exposure is the point. When Grace names the few goals that fit the 12 week frame, the team loses the comfort of pretending every idea is still equally alive. The plan becomes more useful because it becomes less flattering.

reviewCards.front: Your annual plan has ten priorities. What should you retrieve first?
reviewCards.back: Retrieve the selection rule: choose the few goals and actions that can govern the next 12 weeks.

reviewCards.front: Why can a bigger annual plan weaken execution?
reviewCards.back: Size can hide tradeoffs. A broad annual plan lets too many promises stay alive without proof.

reviewCards.front: What makes a 12 week plan different from a wish list?
reviewCards.back: It names near goals, actions, and proof. It changes the week rather than preserving a distant intention.

reviewCards.front: A team wants to keep every goal active. What question helps?
reviewCards.back: Ask which goal can receive real action inside 12 weeks and what must wait.

reviewCards.front: What long-term element should survive when the annual execution plan is cut?
reviewCards.back: The long direction can stay. The loose annual execution plan is what gets replaced.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The core skill is selective planning. You keep long direction but replace the bloated annual execution plan with a few goals and actions that can govern the next 12 weeks.

ifThenPlans.plan: If an annual plan has more priorities than the next 12 weeks can hold, then cut it to the few goals with named actions.
If a team resists dropping goals, then ask which actions will actually happen before the next review.
If your yearly goal feels inspiring but vague, then write the first 12 week result and the next action.
If a plan does not change this week, then rewrite it until one action has a date and owner.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Take one annual plan and cross out every listed action that would not matter inside the next 12 weeks.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, check whether the plan selected real action or merely preserved options. Tighten the plan until the next week knows what to do.
